extracted.intended_audience: EPA decisionmakers, environmental lawyers, and administrative law judges
extracted.subtask_short: notice-and-comment legal comment on EPA rule
extracted.subtask_description: A detailed legal comment submitted in notice-and-comment rulemaking challenging EPA's proposed repeal of an endangerment finding under Section 202 of the Clean Air Act, arguing statutory interpretation, administrative-law, and precedent-based standards. Intended to persuade regulators, appellate courts, or rulemaking record reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual fidelity — do not read 'exposure' into Section 202
rubrics_metrics.description: Nowhere in Section 202 does Congress refer to 'exposure' (or 'inhalation,' 'contact,' 'smog,' or 'acid rain'); omission of such terms must be presumed intentional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An interpretation that requires harms to arise 'through exposure' departs from the plain text. If Congress wanted to limit Section 202 to harms from direct exposure it could have said so; agencies must not magic such a requirement into the statute. See Russello v. United States; compare usage of 'exposure' elsewhere in the Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect and apply statutory definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Act defines terms applicable to a provision (e.g., Section 302(h)'s definition of 'welfare' including adverse effects on weather and climate), those definitions govern interpretation of the provision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency interpretations must account for and be consistent with statutory definitions (e.g., 'welfare' covers climate impacts 'whether caused by transformation, conversion, or combination with other air pollutants'). Agencies cannot ignore or reinterpret those statutory definitions without justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory definitions control over dictionary or ordinary meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: When Congress provides an express statutory definition, that definition is 'virtually conclusive' and overrides contrary contemporary lay-dictionary meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA cannot substitute or prioritize outside dictionaries for definitions the Act provides (Kirtz; Sturgeon). Even for undefined terms, specialized statutory meanings or terms of art may prevail. Agencies must explain any departure from statutory definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate meaningful distinctions when grouping pollutants
rubrics_metrics.description: Labels such as 'local,' 'regional,' or 'global' must reflect meaningful distinctions that allow rational line-drawing between pollutant categories and bear on the statute's scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely applying broad labels without showing how they affect statutory coverage is insufficient. The agency must show that those labels 'serve to rationally group the pollutants' and affect Section 202's reach; otherwise the proposal is arbitrary and capricious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not import common-law tort proximate-cause principles absent statutory text
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles of proximate cause from tort law are not appropriate background rules for interpreting statutory contribution tests unless the statute indicates such incorporation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 202 sets its own causal standards ('cause[] or contribute[] significantly' and whether the air pollution 'may reasonably be anticipated to endanger'). Agencies cannot rewrite those standards by importing tort doctrines; if relying on such principles, the agency must show they are applicable to the statute's framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adhere to precedent and grapple with binding case law
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency must acknowledge and either follow or distinguish controlling judicial precedent (e.g., Massachusetts v. EPA, Catawba Cnty., Ethyl Corp.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposals that conflict with Supreme Court holdings (Massachusetts) or controlling circuit precedent must explain why they are not bound by that precedent. Failure to grapple with relevant case law renders a proposal arbitrary and capricious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasoned explanation requirement (State Farm standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: The agency must 'examine the relevant data and articulate a satisfactory explanation for its action including a rational connection between the facts found and the choice made.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the agency reaches a result that is illogical on its own terms, or fails to explain its reasoning or supporting evidence, the action is arbitrary and capricious. The record must support intermediate factual findings and causal inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precautionary statutory standard: 'may reasonably be anticipated to endanger'
rubrics_metrics.description: The Clean Air Act's 'may reasonably be anticipated to endanger' language permits precautionary judgments about future harms when setting standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's interpretation must respect the statute's precautionary framing; evidence and projections can justify regulation even if harms are incremental or part of a cumulative process. Congressional history (1977 amendments) ratifies this precautionary approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret 'cause or contribute' to include partial contributors
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress intended 'cause or contribute' to capture both sources solely responsible for a pollution problem and sources responsible for only a share of that problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not construe 'contribute' to require sole or major causation. Agency rules or findings should include sources that 'exacerbate' or partially contribute to an air pollution problem (see H.R. Rep. 95-294 and Catawba Cnty.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Support intermediate causal steps with evidence (Ethyl Corp. principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: If intermediate steps in a causal chain are supported by the evidence, the overall regulatory conclusion can be a reasonable hypothesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must provide record evidence for each link in a causal chain (e.g., emissions -> environmental transformation -> harm). Ethyl Corp. shows courts will uphold findings supported by evidence on intermediate steps, even if other sources also contribute to harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for scientific mechanisms and pollutant-specific causal analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Causation analysis must reflect the physical and chemical characteristics of pollutants (e.g., greenhouse gases are globally well-mixed and have direct radiative forcing; NOX/VOCs form ozone via complex interactions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency causal reasoning should not treat different pollutants by rote; it must use appropriate scientific analysis showing how emissions lead to harm. For well-mixed pollutants, the causal chain may be simpler and location of emission less relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid creating statutory limitations the text lacks
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency may not manufacture textual limitations (e.g., excluding global pollutants) that the statute does not contain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretations that add requirements or carve-outs absent from the statutory text are arbitrary. The agency must ground any limiting reading in text, structure, or clear congressional intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on inapposite dictionary definitions to override statutory context
rubrics_metrics.description: Using lay dictionaries to narrow statutory terms is inappropriate where doing so conflicts with the statute's language, definitions, or purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dictionary definitions may be inapposite; courts will not deviate from express statutory definitions merely because they vary from ordinary meaning. Agencies must explain why a dictionary meaning should displace statutory text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major questions doctrine requires clear congressional authorization for transformative agency action
rubrics_metrics.description: The major questions doctrine is a tool of statutory interpretation applied rarely where agency assertions represent 'transformative expansion' of authority and thus require clear congressional authorization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An agency invoking major-questions limits must show the present rule involves the sort of extraordinary delegation that doctrine targets. Prior controlling decisions (e.g., Massachusetts) can preclude invoking the doctrine to limit established regulatory authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain departures from prior agency positions
rubrics_metrics.description: When an agency reverses a long-standing position, it must provide a reasoned explanation for the change, especially where prior positions were informed by the same precedents now cited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mere change in policy preference is insufficient; the agency must address reliance interests, prior analyses, and why the new interpretation is permissible and better supported by law and evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherence across pollutant regulatory regimes — avoid arbitrary differential treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency must coherently justify treating one class of pollutants differently from others regulated under the same or similar statutory provisions (e.g., greenhouse gases vs NOX/VOCs/PM/VOCs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the agency's rationale would also exclude pollutants it admits it can regulate, or fails to distinguish comparable causal chains, that incoherence supports a finding of arbitrariness. The record should explain why differential treatment is rational and consistent with statutory aims.
